Financial advice bills: compare monthly and asset-linked fees with outside cash

Four charts separate Canadian advice-source statistics from hypothetical project, monthly and asset-linked charges, then test the outside cash assigned to each schedule.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Budget three hypothetical fee schedules without assigning an investment benefit

Interactive planning lab

One-time project: total selected fees$2,500
Monthly retainer: total selected fees$4,800
Asset-linked charge: total selected fees$6,400

The first figure contains fixed survey observations. The other figures compare three independent hypothetical payment schedules in CAD, not quotations or equivalent service packages. The project is paid at time zero and has no automatic renewal. Ongoing bills occur at each month-end after the entered outside-cash addition. The asset-linked bill uses a fixed asset base and one-twelfth of the annual percentage; it is paid from outside cash and never deducted from those assets. No portfolio return, promised advice benefit, tax, sales tax, product fee, commission, minimum charge, tiering or cancellation rule is calculated. Negative outside cash is an unmet funding need, not automatic borrowing. A lower cost does not establish adequate scope, quality, suitability or better outcomes.

The central idea

A popular advice source is not a price quote. Compare the written service scope, translate the full fee into dollars and place its due dates beside cash that can actually pay it.

01

Read advice-source use without turning it into a quality ranking

FCAC’s 2024 survey summary supplies the first chart’s eight advice-source percentages. They add to 142%, reflecting overlapping source use. Treat them as mentions, rather than eight slices of one 100% total. The chart measures neither prices nor provider quality.

A source someone consults is different from the work a household needs completed. A budgeting conversation, a retirement projection and implementation of an investment account can involve different tasks, responsibilities and charges. Write the question to be answered before comparing the amount on an invoice.

The fee controls below start a separate exercise. They do not estimate what survey respondents paid or attach a financial outcome to any of the survey’s categories. Editing a fee leaves the historical bars unchanged.

02

Specify the work before comparing payment labels

The age-group and project-review guide examines different survey cuts and the present cost of periodic reviews. Here the focus is a monthly retainer, a fixed asset-based bill and the outside cash that funds those invoices.

A one-time project and an ongoing engagement need not provide the same service. A project may end after a defined report or meeting. An ongoing arrangement may include scheduled updates, access between reviews or implementation work. Those details need written confirmation rather than an assumption based on the billing label.

FCAC’s advisor-selection guide recommends understanding the services, their cost and how payment works. It also suggests asking about qualifications, compensation and the working relationship. Use the actual engagement terms to establish what is included and which questions need another specialist.

In this calculator, the project has no automatic renewal; the retainer continues for every selected month; and the asset-linked charge continues over the same period. These are three hypothetical schedules. The tool does not assert equivalent deliverables, value the advice, or identify which arrangement is suitable.

03

Turn the percentage into dollars using its actual base

The default project costs CAD 2,500 immediately. The alternative retainer costs CAD 200 each month. The third schedule applies an annual 0.8% to an unchanged CAD 400,000 calculation base, divided into twelve monthly bills.

That last calculation is 400,000 × 0.008 = CAD 3,200 a year, or about CAD 266.67 per modeled month. Over the selected twenty-four months, the totals are CAD 2,500, CAD 4,800 and CAD 6,400. The lines reconcile those amounts without assuming an investment return.

The asset figure only calculates a bill. It is not an extra reserve that the cash chart can spend. Every fee in this illustration is paid from outside cash, so the model does not deduct the same charge from the portfolio again. Product expenses, commissions, account charges and taxes are also excluded rather than silently bundled into the selected percentage.

04

Check the first invoice as well as the two-year total

The default outside reserve is CAD 2,000. Another CAD 150 becomes available each month before any recurring bill. The full project fee, however, is due at time zero, before those future additions arrive.

The project’s initial funding gap is CAD 500. Its outside cash later recovers to CAD 3,100 after twenty-four monthly additions. That positive endpoint does not supply the missing cash on the original invoice date. Under the stated order, the project needs CAD 2,500 available at the start.

The retainer uses CAD 50 more than the monthly addition, so its opening-cash requirement over twenty-four months is CAD 1,200. The asset-linked bill uses about CAD 116.67 more each month, requiring CAD 2,800 initially. The entered CAD 2,000 therefore leaves that path CAD 800 short by the end.

These requirements cover only the displayed advice bills. Cash already promised to rent, taxes or another goal cannot also pay these invoices. Negative values identify an unresolved funding need; the calculator does not sell assets, open a credit line or postpone a contractual bill.

05

Use a cost-equivalent asset base as a question, not a verdict

The matrix translates three annual percentages and three unchanging asset bases into annual dollar charges. It helps expose the denominator: the same percentage can produce very different invoices when the amount subject to the fee changes.

At the default 0.8%, CAD 300,000 would produce CAD 2,400 a year, equal in dollars to a CAD 200 monthly retainer. This is a cost-equivalent base for the selected numbers. It does not establish equivalent service or make either structure preferable above or below that amount.

At only three months, the selected retainer totals CAD 600 and the asset-linked schedule CAD 800, while the project still costs CAD 2,500. The thirteenth retainer bill brings cumulative charges to CAD 2,600, passing the project amount. A crossing of selected cash totals does not turn a one-time engagement into thirteen months of support. The horizon and the work promised both matter.

Actual terms can use average balances, quarter-end values, tiered rates, minimum fees or a different billing frequency. Assets can also change through markets, deposits and withdrawals. The model holds the base fixed to isolate the arithmetic. Before using a real percentage, confirm which assets enter the base and whether additional charges apply.

06

Bring a complete fee calendar into the household plan

Record the initial amount, recurring amount, billing dates and expected length of the engagement. Identify any separately quoted follow-up, implementation or product costs. Ask how a change in scope or an end to the relationship affects future invoices and work already paid for.

Keep a separate list of deliverables and responsibilities: what information will be reviewed, what written output is expected, who implements changes, and when the plan is revisited. A cheaper bill cannot answer those questions, and a more expensive bill cannot establish better results.

The calculator deliberately assigns no extra return, tax saving or avoided loss to an advisor. A claim about financial benefits needs evidence of its own and cannot be reverse-engineered from the fee. Start with a clear task and a complete quote, then reconcile the chosen payment schedule with the rest of the household’s commitments.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first chart is a dated FCAC survey extract. The fee schedules, cash ledger and matrix are independent hypothetical calculations; no provider or service package is priced or recommended. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FCAC · Spotlight on Canadians’ use of financial advice ↗

    Issued 17 November 2025; page modified 21 November 2025; reviewed 25 October 2026. Eight overall 2024 CFCS advice-source observations. Category use overlaps; recent-advice and payment questions have separate bases. No sample counts, confidence intervals or causal benefit estimates are constructed.

  2. FCAC · Advice survey news release ↗

    Dated 17 November 2025 and reviewed 25 October 2026. Corroborates the spotlight’s issue date and survey period. Separate recent-advice percentages on this release are not combined with the overall-source chart.

  3. FCAC · Choosing a financial advisor ↗

    Live public HTML reviewed 25 October 2026 for questions on service, cost, compensation and the working relationship. Every fee is hypothetical. The modeled asset-linked charge is one separate assumed charge; it is not a calculation of a product’s MER or an all-in cost.
